# 🌳 What is a Decision Tree?

## The big idea

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
- A series of **yes/no questions** about your data.
- Each answer sends you down a branch.
- At the bottom of the tree, you land on a **prediction**.
- That's it. No math degree required.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](img/tree_example.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🎯 You already do this every day: *"Is it raining? Is the road wet? → take an umbrella."*
:::

---

## You already use trees

::: {.incremental}
- 🏥 **ER triage**: *"Chest pain? → ECG → troponin? → cath lab vs floor."*
- 🏦 **Loan approval**: *"Income > X? → credit score > Y? → approve."*
- 📞 **Customer support menu**: *"Press 1 for billing, 2 for tech support…"*
- 🌳 A **decision tree** just learns the questions **automatically from data**. 🤖
:::

---

## Trees do classification *and* regression

::: {.incremental}
- **Classification trees** → leaves predict a **class** (Yes / No, A / B / C).
- **Regression trees** → leaves predict a **number** (price, BMI, GPA).
- Today we focus on **classification**. The mechanics are the same.
:::

---

## The fundamental tension ⚖️

::: {.incremental}
- 🌱 **Tiny tree** → high bias, misses important patterns. *"It always predicts No."*
- 🌳 **Huge tree** → high variance, memorizes the training set. *"Perfect on train, garbage on test."*
- 🎯 The art is finding the **right size** — and that's what tuning is for.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Sound familiar?
This is the **bias-variance trade-off** from yesterday morning. Trees are the *poster child* for it.
:::
:::

# 🤔 How does the tree choose splits?

## Entropy — measuring "messiness"

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- **Entropy** = how *mixed up* a group is.
- Pure group (all "yes") → entropy = 0. ✅
- 50/50 mix → entropy is at its **maximum**.
- The tree wants to make groups **as pure as possible**.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.fragment}
> 🎯 **YRBS example**
> If a node has 50 students who texted-and-drove and 50 who didn't → **chaos**.
> If it has 95 / 5 → **almost pure**, very informative.
:::
:::
:::

---

## Information Gain — the rule for picking splits

::: {.incremental}
- For each candidate question (e.g. *"Drinks alcohol? Yes/No"*), the algorithm asks:
  > *"How much **less messy** are the two groups after this split?"*
- That reduction in entropy = **Information Gain**.
- The tree picks the split with the **biggest gain** — and repeats.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For the math fans 🤓
Information Gain = *parent entropy* − *weighted average entropy of children*.
The base algorithm is called **ID3**. The `rpart` engine uses a close cousin called the **Gini index** by default — same spirit, different formula.

📘 [A Simple Explanation of Information Gain and Entropy](https://victorzhou.com/blog/information-gain/)
:::
:::

# 🎛️ How big should the tree be?

## Three knobs at a glance

| Knob | What it does | Effect on tree |
|---|---|---|
| `tree_depth` | Caps how **deep** the tree can grow | smaller depth → smaller tree |
| `min_n` | Minimum **rows** required to split a node | larger `min_n` → smaller tree |
| `cost_complexity` ($\alpha$) | **Penalty** added per leaf | larger $\alpha$ → smaller tree |

::: {.fragment}
> The first two stop the tree **early** (during growing). The third **prunes** it after it grows. 🌿✂️
:::

---

## `tree_depth` — early stopping

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Cap the **maximum depth** of the tree.
- Shallow trees can't memorize the training set.
- A simple, blunt way to fight overfitting.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](img/tree_depth1.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
:::

::: {.footer}
[Tune better models](https://tmv.netlify.app/site/slides/rmed03-tune.html#25)
:::

---

## `tree_depth` — visually

![](img/tree_depth2.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

::: {.footer}
[Tune better models](https://tmv.netlify.app/site/slides/rmed03-tune.html#25)
:::

---

## `min_n` — the other early stop

::: {.incremental}
- Minimum number of **observations** required for a node to be split further.
- `min_n = 1` → the tree will keep splitting until every leaf has 1 row. **Pure overfit.** 🚨
- `min_n = 40` → no split unless there are 40+ rows → smaller, simpler tree.
- Useful when classes are imbalanced — keeps the tree from carving out tiny weird leaves.
:::

::: {.footer}
[Tune better models](https://tmv.netlify.app/site/slides/rmed03-tune.html#25)
:::

---

## `cost_complexity` — pruning ✂️

::: {.incremental}
- Grow the tree **all the way**, then snip back the branches that don't pay off.
- Add a penalty $\alpha$ for **every leaf** in the tree.
- Closer to **0** → larger trees survive.
- Larger $\alpha$ → only the most useful splits remain.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The math (optional 🤓)
$$
R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha\,|\widetilde{T}|
$$

- $R(T)$ = misclassification rate of tree $T$
- $|\widetilde{T}|$ = number of **leaves** in $T$
- $\alpha = 0$ → biggest tree wins
- $\alpha \to \infty$ → tree of size 1 wins
:::
:::

::: {.footer}
[PSU — Applied Data Mining](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/lesson/11/11.8/11.8.2)
:::

---

![](img/cost_complex2.png){.fragment fig-align="center" width="70%"}
:::

# 💻 Trees with `tidymodels`

## Today's task 🎯

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
> **Among adolescents, can a decision tree predict whether they have ever consumed alcohol?** 🍺

::: {.incremental}
- **Outcome**: `UsedAlcohol` (binary: Yes / No)
- **Predictors**: every other risky-behavior item in YRBS
- **Model**: classification tree (`rpart`)
- **Why a tree?** It will give us a **picture** we can hand to a clinician — not just a coefficient table.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](https://media.giphy.com/media/JzujPK0id34qI/giphy.gif){fig-align="center"}
:::
:::

---

## Same 7 steps you already know 🔁

::: {.incremental}
1. **Split** train / test (with `strata =`)
2. **Resample** with V-fold CV
3. **Recipe** for preprocessing
4. **Spec** ← this is the **only** thing that changes today!
5. **Workflow** = recipe + spec
6. **Tune** the hyperparameters with `tune_grid()`
7. `finalize_workflow()` → `last_fit()` → metrics + plots
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 If yesterday made sense, today is *95% the same code*. Pinky promise.
:::

---

## Setup — load packages 📦

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(MLearnYRBSS)
library(janitor)
library(skimr)
library(vip)
library(rpart.plot)

data("riskyBehaviors")
```

---

## Need to install first? 📦

::: {.callout-note}
## One-time install
```r
pak::pak(c(
    "tidymodels", "rpart", "rpart.plot",
    "vip", "janitor", "doParallel",
    "MLearnYRBSS"
))
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 `pak` is faster and smarter than `install.packages()` — handles dependencies in parallel.
:::

---

## 1️⃣ Recode the outcome

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|3|4-9|10|11"
#| output-location: fragment
data("riskyBehaviors")

riskyBehaviors_analysis <-
    riskyBehaviors |>
    mutate(
        UsedAlcohol = case_when(
            AgeFirstAlcohol == 1 ~ 0,
            AgeFirstAlcohol %in% c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) ~ 1,
            .default = NA
        ),
        UsedAlcohol = factor(UsedAlcohol)
    ) |>
    drop_na(UsedAlcohol) |>
    select(-c(AgeFirstAlcohol, DaysAlcohol, BingeDrinking,
              LargestNumberOfDrinks, SourceAlcohol))
```

---

## Why drop those columns? 🚨

::: {.callout-warning}
## Avoid data leakage
`AgeFirstAlcohol`, `DaysAlcohol`, `BingeDrinking`, `LargestNumberOfDrinks`, `SourceAlcohol` are **all about alcohol use**. If we left them in, the tree would just memorize the answer.
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🎯 **Outcome encoding:** `0` = never used alcohol · `1` = has used alcohol.
:::

# 2️⃣ Split + Resample

## Train / test split — stratified

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|3-6|8-9|11"
#| output-location: fragment
set.seed(2023)

alcohol_split <- initial_split(
    riskyBehaviors_analysis,
    strata = UsedAlcohol
)

alcohol_train <- training(alcohol_split)
alcohol_test <- testing(alcohol_split)

alcohol_split
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Why `strata =` again?
Keeps the proportion of `UsedAlcohol` roughly equal in train and test — same logic as Lasso this morning. 🔒
:::
:::

---

## Sanity check — class balance

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Training**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
alcohol_train |>
    tabyl(UsedAlcohol) |>
    adorn_pct_formatting(0) |>
    adorn_totals()
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Testing**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
alcohol_test |>
    tabyl(UsedAlcohol) |>
    adorn_pct_formatting(0) |>
    adorn_totals()
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
> Both sets show the same proportions — `strata =` did its job. ✅
:::

---

## Cross-validation folds

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|3"
#| output-location: fragment
set.seed(2023)

cv_alcohol <- vfold_cv(alcohol_train, v = 10, strata = UsedAlcohol)
cv_alcohol
```

::: {.fragment}
> **10 folds** of the *training* set. Every candidate tree we try will be evaluated on all 10 — the test set stays untouched until the very end.
:::

# 3️⃣ Recipe + Spec + Workflow

## Recipe (preprocessing)

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1-2|3|4"
#| output-location: fragment
alcohol_recipe <-
    recipe(UsedAlcohol ~ ., data = alcohol_train) |>
    step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    step_impute_mean(all_numeric_predictors())

alcohol_recipe
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note}
## Trees don't need fancy preprocessing
- ❌ No `step_normalize()` — trees only care about *order*, not scale.
- ❌ No `step_dummy()` — `rpart` handles factor predictors natively.
- ✅ Imputation still useful: `rpart` can't split on `NA`.
:::
:::

---

## Spec — the **only** thing that changed!

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1-5|6|7|9"
#| output-location: fragment
cart_spec <-
    decision_tree(
        cost_complexity = tune(), # ⬅️ tune
        tree_depth = tune(), # ⬅️ tune
        min_n = tune() # ⬅️ tune
    ) |>
    set_engine("rpart") |>
    set_mode("classification")

cart_spec
```

::: {.fragment}
> Yesterday: `logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet")`.
> Today: same pattern, **different model**. ✨
:::

---

## Workflow — bundle it 🔗

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2|3|4"
#| output-location: fragment
cart_workflow <-
    workflow() |>
    add_recipe(alcohol_recipe) |>
    add_model(cart_spec)

cart_workflow
```

::: {.fragment}
> Recipe + spec, neatly packaged. From here on, the code is **identical** to Lasso. ✨
:::

# 4️⃣ Tune the Tree

## Build the tuning grid

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2|3|4|5"
#| output-location: fragment
tree_grid <- grid_regular(
    cost_complexity(),
    tree_depth(c(2, 5)),
    min_n(),
    levels = 4
)

tree_grid
```

---

## Heads up — this can be slow ⏳

::: {.callout-warning}
## Math of the grid
- 4 × 4 × 4 = **64 candidates**
- × 10 folds = **640 model fits** 🤯
- We'll use `doParallel` to speed it up.
- On Posit Cloud Free, expect **~3–5 minutes**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 **Pro tip:** while learning, set `levels = 3` for a faster turnaround.
:::

---

## Run the tuning ⚙️

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "1|3-9|11"
doParallel::registerDoParallel()

cart_tune <-
    cart_workflow |>
    tune_grid(
        resamples = cv_alcohol,
        grid = tree_grid,
        metrics = metric_set(roc_auc),
        control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE)
    )

doParallel::stopImplicitCluster()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
cart_tune <- readRDS("outputs/cart_tune.rds")
```

::: {.fragment}
> 💡 We use **ROC AUC** as the tuning metric — robust to class imbalance, and the same one we used for Lasso. Consistency = sanity.
:::

---

## Show the best candidates

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
show_best(cart_tune, metric = "roc_auc")
```

::: {.fragment}
> The top 5 hyperparameter combos, ranked by mean ROC AUC across the 10 folds. 🏆
:::

---

## Visualize the tuning results

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| output-location: slide
autoplot(cart_tune)
```

::: {.fragment}
> Each panel shows how the metric changes as one knob varies — colored by the others. Look for the sweet spot. 🍯
:::

---

## Pick the best combo

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1-3"
#| output-location: fragment
best_cart <- select_best(cart_tune, metric = "roc_auc")

best_cart
```

::: {.fragment}
> One row, the winner candidate. **Don't commit yet** — let's check how it actually performs first. 🤔
:::

# 5️⃣ Sanity-Check Before Committing

## How does our chosen candidate *actually* do? 🔍

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2|3|4"
#| output-location: fragment
cart_workflow |>
    finalize_workflow(best_cart) |>
    fit_resamples(resamples = cv_alcohol) |>
    collect_metrics()
```

::: {.fragment}
> An honest, CV-estimated performance for our **single** chosen combo.
:::

---

## 🔄 This is your decision point!

::: {.incremental}
- 😀 **Metrics look good** → lock it in, evaluate on test. ✅
- 😬 **Metrics look bad** → **STOP**. Go back and re-tune. 🛑
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## 🚨 Important
Once you commit with `finalize_workflow()` → `last_fit()`, **you've used your test set**. No going back.
:::
:::

---

## What does "go back and re-tune" mean? 🔧

::: {.incremental}
- Try a **wider** or **finer** grid.
- Add a different **metric** (e.g. `pr_auc` for imbalanced data).
- Revisit your **recipe** — more imputation? feature engineering?
- Try **more folds** in your CV.
- Drop redundant or leaky predictors.
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 **Iterating here is the *job*.** Most "good models" took 5–10 rounds of this loop.
:::

---

## Looks good? Lock it in 🔒

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
cart_final_wf <- finalize_workflow(cart_workflow, best_cart)

cart_final_wf
```

::: {.fragment}
> `finalize_workflow()` swaps the `tune()` placeholders for the actual best values. **Now we're committed.** ✅
:::

# 6️⃣ Evaluate on the Test Set

## `last_fit()` — the magic shortcut ✨

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2-6"
#| output-location: fragment
cart_last_fit <-
    last_fit(
        cart_final_wf,
        split   = alcohol_split,
        metrics = metric_set(accuracy, kap, roc_auc, sensitivity, specificity)
    )

cart_last_fit
```

---

## Why `last_fit()` is so cool 🪄

::: {.callout-tip}
## Same trick as Lasso this morning
- ✅ Fits on **all** training data
- ✅ Predicts on the **test** set
- ✅ Computes metrics — once, honestly
- ✅ No accidental cheating possible
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 One function, one honest answer. **Use it everywhere.**
:::

---

## Test-set metrics

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
collect_metrics(cart_last_fit)
```

::: {.fragment}
> Compare these to the **CV metrics** from the sanity-check slide. If they're in the same ballpark → 🎉 your model generalizes. If test is *much* worse → the tree may have been too tuned to your folds.
:::

---

## Test-set predictions

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
tree_pred <-
    cart_last_fit |>
    collect_predictions() |>
    select(UsedAlcohol, .pred_class, .pred_1, .pred_0)

tree_pred
```

---

## Confusion matrix

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
tree_pred |>
    conf_mat(truth = UsedAlcohol, estimate = .pred_class) |>
    autoplot(type = "heatmap")
```

::: {.fragment}
> Look at the **off-diagonals** — those are the *kinds* of mistakes your tree makes. Are false positives or false negatives more dangerous for your question?
:::

---

## ROC curve on the test set

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| output-location: slide
tree_pred |>
    roc_curve(truth = UsedAlcohol, .pred_1, event_level = "second") |>
    autoplot()
```

::: {.fragment}
> A curve hugging the **top-left corner** = excellent. The diagonal = random guessing. 🎲
:::

# 🌟 The Big Reveal

## Visualize the final tree 🌳

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
#| output-location: slide
cart_last_fit |>
    extract_fit_engine() |>
    rpart.plot(roundint = FALSE, type = 4, extra = 104)
```

::: {.fragment}
> **This** is the superpower of trees: a model your collaborator (or PI, or grandma 👵) can read without a stats degree.
:::

---

## Variable importance with `vip` 🏆

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
#| output-location: slide
cart_last_fit |>
    extract_fit_parsnip() |>
    vip(num_features = 15)
```

---

## How to read the `vip` plot 👀

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you're looking at
- Each bar = how much that predictor **reduced impurity** across all splits.
- Predictors **not shown** were never useful enough to make the tree.
- A free **feature ranking** for your manuscript. 📝
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 `vip` works for **any** `tidymodels` model — Lasso, RF, XGBoost, KNN. Same syntax. ✨
:::

# 🎯 Your Turn

## Step 1 — Set up your page 📄

In your `ml-template`, open **`models/decision-tree.qmd`** and:

::: {.incremental}
1. **Load** your data:
   ```r
   analysis_data <- rio::import("models/data/analysis_data.rds")
   ```
2. Use the **same outcome** you used for logistic regression and Lasso.
3. Copy your **Lasso pipeline** as a starting point. 📋
:::

---

## Step 2 — Swap the spec 🔄

::: {.incremental}
4. Change the spec:
   ```r
   decision_tree(
       cost_complexity = tune(),
       tree_depth      = tune(),
       min_n           = tune()
   ) |>
       set_engine("rpart") |>
       set_mode("classification")
   ```
5. **Drop** `step_normalize()` and `step_dummy()` — trees don't need them.
6. Build the tuning grid (start with `levels = 3` for speed).
:::

---

## Step 3 — Sanity-check, fit, visualize 🌳

::: {.incremental}
7. Add the **CV sanity-check** with `fit_resamples()` before finalizing.
8. Add `last_fit()` + confusion matrix + ROC on the test set.
9. Visualize your tree with **`rpart.plot`** + a **`vip()`** plot.
10. **Render** your website. 🚀
:::

# 🌲 Bridge to Random Forest

## One tree is good. **Five hundred** is better.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- A single tree is **interpretable** but **unstable** — small changes in data → very different tree.
- What if we grew **hundreds** of trees on different bootstrap samples and let them **vote**? 🗳️
- That's a **Random Forest** — and it usually beats one tree, hands down.
- After the break, that's exactly what we'll build. 🌲🌲🌲
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](https://media.giphy.com/media/3o7budMRwZvNGJ3pyE/giphy.gif){fig-align="center"}
:::

# 🎁 Wrapping Up

## What you learned this session

::: {.incremental}
- ✅ A decision tree = a **series of yes/no questions** learned from data.
- ✅ It picks splits using **entropy** + **information gain**.
- ✅ Three knobs control its size: **`tree_depth`**, **`min_n`**, **`cost_complexity`**.
- ✅ The full `tidymodels` flow: split → recipe → spec → workflow → **tune** → finalize → **CV check** → `last_fit()` → metrics → tree plot → `vip`.
- ✅ Trees are **interpretable** — that's their superpower (and their main reason for existing).
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 You've now seen **three** spec swaps (logistic → Lasso → tree) on the **same** pipeline. Random Forest, XGBoost, and KNN are just **three more spec swaps**. 💪
:::

---

## Review questions 🧠

::: {.fragment}
1. Why does a deeper tree usually have **higher variance**?
:::

::: {.fragment}
2. What does **`min_n = 1`** do to the tree, and why is it dangerous?
:::

::: {.fragment}
3. Why don't trees need `step_normalize()`?
:::

::: {.fragment}
4. We compared **CV metrics** vs **test metrics**. What does it mean if they're very different?
:::

::: {.fragment}
5. **Bonus**: when would you choose a single tree **on purpose** over a Random Forest? 🤔
:::
